So I've tested this PR applied to 1.1.1d. 

To test this, I've made the following changes, to make sure
I'm properly testing it:
#undef __NR_getrandom before this line:
if defined(__linux) && !defined(__NR_getrandom)

I've removed the getentropy() call, so that running it against a
newer libc doesn't pick that up.

I've build this in jessies chroots, that contains:
linux-libc-dev 3.16.72-1
libc6-dev 2.19-18+deb8u10

I had successful getrandom call for the following arches:
amd64, armel, armhf and i386

Debian only still supports jessie for the above 4 arches, so the
Debian porter boxes don't have jessie chroots available anymore for
the others it released with: arm64, mips, mipsel, powerpc, ppc64el, s390x

Stretch even dropped powerpc support, and so Debian has no
hosts anymore that still run that. Stretch added support
for mips64el.

So I built this in a stretch chroots with contained the following:
libc6-dev 2.24-11+deb9u4
linux-libc-dev 4.9.189-3+deb9u1

This was tested on the following arches: arm64 mipsel mips64el ppc64 s390x

All hosts were running kernel 4.19.67-2+deb10u1 

(Debian dropped mips support in sid and doesn't have any porterbox for mips left,
but it's the same ABI as mipsel.)

On Sun, Sep 29, 2019 at 05:22:36AM -0700, Kurt Roeckx wrote:
> (Debian dropped mips support in sid and doesn't have any porterbox for mips left,
> but it's the same ABI as mipsel.)

It clearly wasn't true that there is no porterbox anymore, because
I provided data from it yesterday. So I've now also tested mips in
a stretch chroot.


Kurt

issue_context.title: ssl.SSLError: [SSL] malloc failure - with openssl=1.1.1d (ppc64le)
issue_context.body:
I originally commented in this conda issue: https://github.com/ContinuumIO/anaconda-issues/issues/11274, but after a little debug I decided to report the issue here as well.

Currently to reproduce the error I have been using a default conda environment with python 3.6 or 3.7 installed:

```
conda create -y -n my-test-env python=3.6
```
then running the following command
```
python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen("https://pypi.org")'
```
which produces the following error:
```
(my-test-env) [builder@b98996cfec6a ~]$ python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen("https://pypi.org")'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/urllib/request.py", line 223, in urlopen
    return opener.open(url, data, timeout)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/urllib/request.py", line 526, in open
    response = self._open(req, data)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/urllib/request.py", line 544, in _open
    '_open', req)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/urllib/request.py", line 504, in _call_chain
    result = func(*args)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/urllib/request.py", line 1361, in https_open
    context=self._context, check_hostname=self._check_hostname)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/urllib/request.py", line 1286, in do_open
    h = http_class(host, timeout=req.timeout, **http_conn_args)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/http/client.py", line 1392, in __init__
    context = ssl._create_default_https_context()
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/ssl.py", line 502, in create_default_context
    context = SSLContext(PROTOCOL_TLS)
  File "/opt/anaconda3/envs/my-test-env/lib/python3.6/ssl.py", line 391, in __new__
    self = _SSLContext.__new__(cls, protocol)
ssl.SSLError: [SSL] malloc failure (_ssl.c:2805)
```
at this point, I don't have a test case without conda or python, but would be willing to write/test any suggested code to isolate the issue in ppc64le env.

I did poke around a little in the openssl code, using git bisect I narrowed it down to commit openssl/openssl@3ff98f5 as causing the problem, see openssl/openssl#9595 for details on the commit.
I disabled the change by setting -DOPENSSL_RAND_SEED_DEVRANDOM_SHM_ID=-1 as suggested in the PR and was able to run the previously failing test successfully.

I made the following change in build.sh:
```
 diff --git a/recipe/build.sh b/recipe/build.sh
index a6cb10d..2155c45 100644
--- a/recipe/build.sh
+++ b/recipe/build.sh
@@ -29,7 +29,7 @@ if [[ ${_BASE_CC} == *-* ]]; then
       ;;
     *powerpc64le-*linux*)
       _CONFIG_OPTS+=(linux-ppc64le)
-      CFLAGS="${CFLAGS} -Wa,--noexecstack"
+      CFLAGS="${CFLAGS} -Wa,--noexecstack -DOPENSSL_RAND_SEED_DEVRANDOM_SHM_ID=-1"
       ;;
     *darwin*)
```
I don't think I have enough context regarding the change to figure out the root cause.

[openssl-config-data-dump.txt](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/files/3652871/openssl-config-data-dump.txt)

Alright, seems the problem with the outdated kernel headers is not only a theoretical one.
We need to supply our own define here.  I did that for all kernel versions I am able to test with.
I would like that to be done by people who are able to test that specific kernel.

I have access to most if not all architecutes supported by Debian,
so I should be able to test them.

But I think that if we're going to treat 4.8 as special, we should
add the define for all architectures supported by 4.8. Archituctures
added afterwards will always have it in the kernel headers.

Right, the point with v4.8 is that the entropy generator was re-designed in v4.8
due to critics by Daniel Bernstein, and by that re-design it unfortunately broke
the assumption that the /dev/urandom is initialized when /dev/random is readable
for the first time.
I do not think we should add the define's, I think Debian should.  Or we have it in a NOTES file.  Suppose we get the number wrong?

Debian stable and unstable have the proper defines. But there
clearly are people who don't have them.

That's why I did only add syscall numbers which I can personally verify.
I think we should only take the risk for systems which are used really often,
and where bad cross-toolchains are known to be circulating as in this case.

Even oldstable has them. I was planning to do a test building this
on oldstable, but even that is too recent. I need oldoldstable
which ships a 3.16 kernel, and so has 3.16 kernel headers.

(Or I change something so the kernel headers don't get included.)

I only talk about Debian because I have access to all Debian
development machines, and there should be one for each archicture.
At least the release architectures should have one I can just ssh
in, the others might require me ask to set up an account.

The only reasonable way how this can happen is when you are targeting
your cross compiler for an old linux/glibc version, then you have no other
choice than to use linux/glibc headers, and libraries from before 2013.
Once you have this toolchain running it will produce binaries that run
on any system version newer than the sys-root files.
So people will just use it.
IF you do it with brand new glibc files your binaries will only run on
new glibc versions, due to the glibc being only upward compatible
not downward compatible.

I think a NOTES.DEBIAN file created by Kurt who is a Debian maintainer is the best and safest way to go.  It's not hard to add -D__NR_getrandom=359 to your config line.  And there is a risk that someone will get their OS indirectly.  Are we confident, for example, that Ubuntu hasn't changed anything here?
No they won't change that number.

Note that they all run in a chroot/container/whatever that only
has old files. It probably contains an old libc and kernel
headers. But the host system runs a recent kernel. This doesn't
even have to do with cross compilation, just targeting old
systems. And it breaks if you run it on a new kernel.

So people that upgrade the kernel will suddenly see their system
break, because the binary was build on an old system that didn't
know anything about that system call.

I really only see 2 options:
- We add the defines for the system call (for all systems we can test)
- We stop treating 4.8 as something that requires the system call.

Option 1 sounds more safe.
The problem with Option 2 is that reading /dev/random does not
give you a guarantee that the CRNG is properly initialized with 4.8 and above.
Option 3 print something on the console and ask user for permission to continue.
I don't think option 3 is something a library should do.

I was able to build an openssl conda-package using commit https://github.com/openssl/openssl/commit/eee565ec4b8509b53ee280e8f37243bc5cb5f535 and I no longer see the failure I was seeing.

Thank you!
